issuer: Georgia Government Transparency and Campaign Finance Commission
title: Georgia Advisory Opinion 2025-02
text:
Get a PDF of the Advisory Opinion here
In response to an advisory opinion request on July 17, 2025, from Byran Tyson (“Requestor”), the Georgia State Ethics Commission (“Commission”) advises that (a) a candidate may loan personal funds
to
a Leadership Committee or a PAC; (b) the candidate can be repaid with funds raised into the Leadership Committee or PAC and then loan those funds to his or her campaign committee; (c) the answer is the same if the loan to the candidate committee occurs during a primary; and (d) there is insufficient information or facts to answer the hypothetical as to whether any potential liability would be faced by contributors to the Leadership Committee or PAC.
Question Presented in Request for Advisorv Opinion 2025–02
In a letter from Bryan Tyson of Clark Hill PLC
1
, the following questions were presented for an advisory opinion from the Commission:
1. Can a candidate loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC?
2. If a candidate is permitted to loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC and then raises funds without no contribution limit into that entity for purposes of repaying the loan, can the candidate repay him or herself with the unlimited funds raised and then loan those funds to bis or her candidate campaign committee?
3. Does the answer to Question 2 change if the loan to the candidate committee occurs during a primary using funds raised in a leadership committee?
4. If a candidate utilizes a leadership committee or PAC to repay a loan which is then loaned to his or her candidate campaign committee, do contributors to that leadership committee or PAC face potential liability for participating in that effort?
Discussion and Legal Analysis
Pursuant to a written request for an advisory opinion dated July 15, 2025, Bryan Tyson of Clark Hill PLC, seeks guidance as to each of the four questions presented below which will be addressed and discussed in order.
1. Can a candidate loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC?
A leadership committee may receive contributions from persons who are members or supporters of the leadership committee and expend such funds as permitted by this code section.  O.C.G.A. §21-5-34.2(b).  Furthermore, “contribution” is defined in the Georgia Government Transparency and Campaign Finance Act in relevant part as,
“Contribution” means a gift, subscription, membership,
loan,
forgiveness of debt, advance or deposit of money or anything of value conveyed or transferred for the purpose of influencing the nomination for election or election of any person for office, bringing about the recall of a public officer holding elective office or opposing the recall of a public officer holding elective office, or the influencing of voter approval or rejection of a proposed constitutional amendment, a state- wide referendum, or a proposed question which is to appear on the ballot in this state or in a county or a municipal election in this state … ” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(7) (emphasis added).
The requester cites O.C.G.A. § 21-5-33(a) in his analysis of whether a candidate can loan personal funds to a leadership committee or PAC.  However, the language of that section refers to the disposition of contributions received by the candidate, a campaign committee, or a public officer. That section states that the disposition of those contributions received by the candidate, campaign committee, or a public officer, shall only be used to defray ordinary and necessary expenses incurred in connection with such candidate’s campaign for elective office or such public officer’s fulfillment or retention of such office. There is nothing to suggest in this section that appears to limit the ability of a candidate to loan personal funds to either a PAC or a Leadership Committee. See O.C.G.A. § 21-5-33(a).
It should be noted that a candidate can personally make unlimited contributions (
or loans)
to his or her own campaign or campaign committee. Pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 21-5-41 (g), the contribution limitations established by this Code shall not apply to a loan or other contributions made to a campaign committee or candidate by the candidate or a member of the family of the candidate.
In summary, a candidate can loan personal funds to a Leadership Committee or a PAC. There is nothing in the current statute which prohibits such a loan of personal funds.
2. If a candidate is permitted to loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC, and then raises funds without no contribution limit into that entity for purposes of repaying the loan, can the candidate repay him or herself with the unlimited funds raised and then loan those funds to his or her candidate campaign committee?
If a candidate is loaning personal funds to a Leadership Committee or PAC and then the loan is repaid back to the candidate, the repayment of the loan back to the candidate is in effect repaying the candidate with his or her own funds. The candidate is free to loan his or her funds to the Leadership Committee or a PAC. The candidate is free to loan his or her funds to their campaign committee.
In the hypothetical scenario posed by the Requester the candidate makes a personal loan of $500,000 to a PAC which then receives two contributions of $250,000 from individual donors made to the same PAC. The PAC repays the loan to the candidate who then loans his or her candidate committee $500,000. The Requester suggests that this is a way of funneling unlimited contributions into the candidate campaign committee through the loan arrangement. This suggested scenario seems to disregard that the only money being repaid to the candidate is the same personal money which the candidate already possessed and thus is only receiving back. This is not a contribution to the candidate; this is just the repayment of a loan (the candidate’s own money) which the candidate made and is entitled to receive. This is a zero net gain for the candidate.
According to the Act, the contribution limitations established by this Code shall not apply to a loan or other contributions made to a campaign committee or candidate by the candidate or a member of the family of the candidate. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-4l(g).
3. Does the answer to Question 2 change if the loan to the candidate committee occurs during a primary using funds raised in a leadership committee?
No. The loan to the candidate committee can be made with whatever personal funds the candidate chooses to use whether during a primary or general election. The Leadership Committee in this scenario has paid back the loan to the candidate, the repayment of which has not increased the availability of personal funds to the candidate, who then loans the funds to the campaign committee. The candidate has not obtained any additional money from the Leadership Committee but only the candidate’s own money which is being repaid.
4. If a candidate utilizes a leadership committee or PAC to repay a loan which is then loaned to his or her candidate campaign committee, do contributors to that leadership committee or PAC face potential liability for participating in that effort?
As was already discussed, the money in this scenario is and always was the candidate’s own money and there is no liability for a candidate to loan money to his or her campaign committee. This hypothetical does not provide sufficient information or facts upon which to answer the question put forth regarding contributors.
The Georgia State Ethics Commission advises that a candidate may loan personal funds to a Leadership Committee or a PAC. Additionally, a candidate is permitted to be repaid back that loan from the Leadership Committee or PAC and then use those funds to make a loan to his or her candidate campaign committee as the candidate is only receiving back his or her own money.
The Commission further advises whether this loan takes place during a primary or general election has no bearing on the matter and does not change the analysis.  This Advisory Opinion concerns the application of the Georgia Government Transparency and Campaign Finance Act, or regulations prescribed by the Georgia State Ethics Commission, to the specific facts, transaction, or activity set forth for Advisory Opinion 2025-02.
Advisory Opinion 2025-02 is hereby adopted by the Commission in conformity with O.C.G.A.
§
21-5-6(13) on December 4

Re:        Request for Advisory Opinion
Dear Director Emadi:
I write to request a written advisory opinion from the Ethics Commission in accordance -with O.C.G.A. § 21-5-6(b)(13) within 60 days as required by the statutory structure. This request is written on behalf of a statewide candidate.
Under Georgia law, candidates may only have a single campaign committee and contributions to that committee are limited.  O.C.G.A. §§ 21-5-30, 21-5-41; Commission Advisory Opinion 2017-05. Georgia lawalso provides for other types of campaign-related entities, like leadership committees, O.C.G.A. § 21-5-34.2, and political action committees, O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(20). Political action committees are not candidate campaign committees.
Id.
Further, leadership committees are separate from a candidate’s campaign committee.  O.C.G.A.
§
21-5-34.2(a), (f).  Specifically, a campaign committee is an entity that “accepts contributions or makes expenditures designed to bring about the nomination or election of an individual to any elected office.” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(2).
Georgia law provides an exception to contribution limits for loans “made to a
campaign committee
or candidate by the candidate or a member of the farnily
1
of the candidate.” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-41(g) (emphasis added). But this exception is narrow, because it only applies to “a campaign committee” and apparently not to other types of campaign related entities under Georgia law.
Id.
It is the intersection of these areas about which we seek direction from the Commission on the following four questions.
QUESTIONS PRESENTED
Can a candidate loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC?
If a candidate is permitted to loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC and then raises funds without no contribution limit into that entity for purposes of repaying the loan, can the candidate repay him- or herself with the unlimited funds raised and then. loan those funds to his or her candidate campaign committee?
Does the answer to Question 2 change if the loan to the candidate committee occurs during a primary using funds raised in a leadership committee?
If a candidate utilizes a leadership committee or PAC to repay a loan which is then loaned to his or her candidate campaign committee, do contributors to that leadership committee or PAC face potential liability for participating in that effort?
ANALYSIS
Can a candidate loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC?
As to the first question, the relevant statutory language indicates that a candidate is prohibited from loaning funds to a non-candidate committee of any type, because both a leadership committee and a PAC are not “campaign committees” under Georgia law.  Leadership committees are defined as a particular “committee, corporation, or organization” chaired by certain individuals and is explicitly defined as being “a separate legal entity from a candidate’s campaign committee.” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-34.2(a), (f). Likewise, the definition of a PAC “does not include a candidate campaign committee.” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(20).
Further, a candidate can only use contributions to repay loans made by the candidate
“to the campaign committee
of
such candidate
or such public officer, incurred in connection with such candidate’s campaign for elective office … ” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-33(a) (emphasis added).  These provisions read together indicate that a candidate cannot loan funds to any type of entity except for his or her designated candidate committee. As a result, it appears that a candidate cannot make loans under Georgia law to a PAC or a leadership committee.
If a candidate is permitted to loan personal funds to a leadership committee or a PAC and then raises funds without no contribution limit into that entity for purposes of repaying the loan, can the candidate repay him- or herself with the unlimited funds raised and then loan those funds to his or her candidate campaign committee?
The answer to second question also appears to be no, because if a candidate was permitted to make loans to leadership committees and PACs, then the candidate can avoid contribution limits altogether. This is because a candidate could loan a large amount to a leadership committee or PAC, then raise unlimited funds to repay that loan back to the candidate. The candidate would then be able to tum around and loan those same funds to this or her candidate campaign committee-an arrangement that would allow this flow-through to wash away contribution limits entirely.
Imagine this scenario: A candidate loans a PAC a sum of $500,000, then requests two contributions of $250,000 from wealthy donors because contributions to a PAC are not limited. Once those are paid, the candidate can repay the personal loan made to the PAC, and then loan her candidate committee $500,000, funneling the unlimited contributions into the candidate campaign committee through the loan arrangement.
Thus, if the Commission considers leadership committees and PACs as “campaign committees” for purposes of candidate loans or considers otherwise that leadership committees and PA Cs can accept loans from any source as a “contribution,” then it appears that a candidate would be eligible to repay him- or herself with unlimited funds raised in a leadership committee or PAC. The candidate could then loan those funds raised without limits to his or her candidate committee in an unlimited amount. This is because the contribution limits do not apply to loans ·made to a candidate campaign committee “by the candidate or a member of the family of the candidate.” O.C.G.A.
§
21-5-41(g).
This approach appears to be prohibited by existing Georgia law, because candidate loans are restricted to a single type of entity-a candidate campaign committee-so that this type of situation cannot occur and candidates must only raise funds with limits to repay any loans.
Does the answer to Question 2 change if the loan to the candidate committee occurs during a primary using funds raised in a leadership committee?
As the Commission is aware, in 2022, a federal court found that leadership committees could not be used to create different contribution limits in a primary where one candidate had access to a leadership committee and the other did not.
Perdue v. Kemp,
584 F. Supp. 3d 1310, 1323 (N.D. Ga. 2022). Thus,· if a candidate with a leadership committee was able to loan money to a leadership committee, raise unlimited funds to repay that loan, and then loan those same funds to the candidate’s campaign committee, it appears that the same First Amendment violation present in
Perdue
would also occur because one candidate would face State Ethics Commission no contribution limits while the other candidate would be limited, especially if a loan was permitted to a leadership committee and not to a PAC.
If a candidate utilizes a leadership committee or PAC to repay a loan which is then loaned to his or her candidate campaign committee, do contributors to that leadership committee or PAC face potential liability for participating in that effort?
Georgia law places obligations on both donors and candidates for compliance with the contribution-limit provisions of the Code, because it specifically sets forth the dual mandate that contributors shall not “make” excess contributions and that candidates shall not “receive” such contributions. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-41(a). If a contributor gave to a leadership committee or PAC aware that a loan arrangement was being used to raise unlimited funds that could be moved to a candidate campaign committee in a primary election, the contributor would then be on notice of the excess nature of the contribution, or at the very least its potential use beyond the candidate contribution limits. If the contribution and loan took place in the primary involving a leadership committee, the contributor would also be on notice of the attempt to avoid the results of
Perdue,
584 F. Supp. 3d at 1323, because the arrangement would effectively provide different contribution limits for candidates in the primary election.
Given the Commission’s ability to enforce campaign finance laws and the disclosed nature of the contribution, the Commission would then be able to investigate any effort to raise funds into a leadership committee or PAC during a primary election for purposes of avoiding contribution limits, including any donors who participated aware of that structure.
1
The family of the candidate is defined as spouse and dependent children, not other family members. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(17).
******
Thank you for your time and consideration of these important issues. Given the proliferation of various entities supporting candidates that are not candidate committees, it is important that the Commission clarify these rules quickly, but no later than the 60-day period required in the statute.
Sincerely,
Bryan P. Tyson
